items.title: Blood pressure and glaucoma.
items.abstract: Intraocular pressure (IOP) remains the only modifiable risk factor in glaucoma, yet many patients continue to progress despite adequate IOP control. Systemic blood pressure (BP) has re-emerged as a candidate IOP-independent vascular risk factor. This review synthesizes current evidence on the relationship between BP and glaucoma, with particular attention to recent literature describing circadian BP patterns, short- and long-term BP variability, and minimum ambulatory BP values. Both elevated and reduced BP have been associated with glaucoma development and progression, consistent with a bimodal relationship mediated by ocular perfusion pressure. Beyond absolute BP level, recent studies using 24-h ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) have identified nocturnal over-dipping, high 24-h and long-term BP variability, and, most notably, the minimum BP nadir as independent predictors of structural and functional glaucomatous progression, often outperforming mean BP values in multivariable models. Office-based BP measurements correlate poorly with 24-h ABPM specifically among patients with the lowest BP readings, suggesting isolated office readings may fail to capture clinically relevant hypotensive exposure. Emerging evidence further indicates that BP-related vulnerability is not uniform across the eye: the focal ischemic optic disc phenotype and the central visual field each appear disproportionately susceptible to the effects of low or unstable BP compared with generalized cup enlargement phenotypes or the peripheral field, respectively. The relationship between BP and glaucoma is more complex than a simple linear or threshold-based association, encompassing absolute level, circadian pattern, variability, and minimum values, each of which may independently influence disease course. Twenty-four-hour ABPM may offer meaningful prognostic value beyond office-based measurement, particularly in patients progressing despite controlled IOP, and clinicians should maintain a low threshold to pursue such monitoring and to coordinate BP management with primary care or cardiology colleagues in this population.

items.title: Benchmarking heart failure care: the ANZACS-QI Heart Failure Registry Pilot implementation and results (ANZACS-QI 86).
items.abstract: Heart failure is a major healthcare problem in Aotearoa New Zealand. As therapies advance and become increasingly complex it is essential that we systematically characterise phenotype and monitor adherence to relevant guidelines to drive quality improvement. Here we report the results of the ANZACS-QI Heart Failure Registry Pilot, implemented in Northern Region hospitals. Age-stratified random sampling was used to identify a representative cohort of patients hospitalised with heart failure (2022 and 2023) using national administrative datasets. The electronic clinical records were reviewed and data entered into the web-based registry. Pre-specified outcomes that were analysed included rates of left ventricular assessment (left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]) and prescription of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). The cohort comprised 328 patients and registry form completion rates were high (98%). LVEF assessment rates within 2 years of the index hospital discharge were 81%. Of those with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that survived until discharge (n=137), only 13 (9%) met the composite medication indicator of being prescribed (or with documented contraindication/intolerance) all four GDMT classes. This was largely driven by 92 (67%) being ineligible for subsidy for sodium glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors; however, prescription rates of the other GDMT classes were suboptimal. Our study highlights that there is a considerable gap between guideline recommendations and real-world practice. Following pilot completion, performance indicators have been established and the registry has expanded with the goal for it to become national. The successful implementation of the registry is an important step in quality improvement for patients hospitalised with heart failure.

items.title: Mapping Mesoscale Cardiac Architecture With Axially Swept Dithered Light-Sheet Microscopy.
items.abstract: Comprehensive characterization of cardiac microstructure and vascular networks is critical for assessing cardiovascular development, disease progression, and therapeutic interventions. While volumetric imaging combined with tissue clearing enables high-resolution organ-level analysis, the densely organized cardiac microenvironment, characterized by compacted and trabeculated myocardium, remains technically challenging to resolve in its entirety. To address these limitations, we exploit the temporal dynamics of illumination-detection interplay to create a time-averaged beam profile, thereby maximizing system throughput across multi-scale specimens. Our dithered light-sheet (DiLS) approach extends the confocal region by over 40% and improves the space-bandwidth product while largely preserving optical sectioning capability. Building on this, the axially swept dithered light-sheet (AS-DiLS) employs a dual-actuator strategy that combines rapid beam dithering and axial sweeping to further accelerate imaging speed while achieving micrometer-scale resolution across centimeter-scale scanning ranges, enabling detailed cardiovascular morphological and topological assessment from embryonic to adult stages. We anticipate that this scalable imaging scheme will advance in-depth investigations of organ morphogenesis and disease pathogenesis across a broad spectrum of models.

items.title: Screening for Cardiac Amyloidosis in Men with Angina and Non-Obstructive Coronary Finding: The CHEST-CA study.
items.abstract: Background Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) may cause microvascular dysfunction leading to chest pain, even in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Whether angina in older men may represent an early clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed CA remains unknown Methods In this prospective multicenter study, 150 men aged ≥65 years presenting with chest pain were recruited from three outpatient cardiology clinics in the Capital Region of Denmark. All par-ticipants had non-obstructive findings on coronary imaging by either cardiac computed to-mography angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging. A systematic screening protocol in-cluded clinical evaluation, electrocardiography, echocardiography, blood and urine tests for monoclonal proteins, and cardiac scintigraphy. ATTR-CA was defined by Perugini grade ≥2 myocardial uptake in the absence of monoclonal gammopathy. Results The median age was 72.6 years (IQR: 68.8-77.4). Most patients underwent perfusion imaging (63.0%) prior to inclusion. Median high-sensitive troponin T was 12.0 ng/L (IQR, 9.0-18.0), and median NT-proBNP was 173.9 ng/L (IQR 81.9-459.9). Heart failure was present in 24.0% and atrial fibrillation or flutter in 39.7% of patients. In total, two patients (1.3%; 95% CI 0.2- 4.%) were diagnosed with wild-type transthyretin CA with grade 3 cardiac uptake. One patient had manifest cardiomyopathy, and the second CA patient had normal cardiac biomarkers and echocardiography and was surveilled. Conclusions Among elderly men with suspected cardiac angina and non-obstructive coronary findings, the prevalence of undiagnosed ATTR-CA was low (1.3%). Additional enrichment criteria may be necessary to improve diagnostic yield, but this remains hypothesis-generating.

items.title: Self-reported decreased libido in patients evaluated for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): Association with depressive symptoms rather than OSA severity.
items.abstract: BackgroundSexual health complaints are frequently reported by patients evaluated for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) but remain under-recognized in respiratory care settings. The relative contributions of respiratory disease severity, daytime symptoms, and psychological factors to decreased libido in this population remain poorly understood.ObjectivesThe aim of the study was to determine the prevalence of self-reported decreased libido in patients evaluated for suspected or confirmed OSA and to identify factors independently associated with this complaint.DesignMonocentric cross-sectional observational study performed in patients referred for suspected or confirmed obstructive sleep apnea from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025.MethodsSelf-reported decreased libido was assessed using a dichotomous patient-reported measure. Demographic characteristics, body mass index, comorbidities, OSA severity indices, daytime sleepiness, fatigue, and depressive symptoms were collected using standardized clinical assessments and questionnaires. Multivariable logistic regression models were performed to identify factors independently associated with decreased libido, including models based on directed acyclic graph (DAG) confounder selection, extended models including symptoms, sex-stratified analyses, and formal testing of sex-by-depression interaction.ResultsAmong 188 included patients (mean age 55.3 ± 15.9 years; 64.4% women), self-reported decreased libido was reported by 44.7%. In multivariable analyses based on DAG-selected confounders, increasing age was independently associated with decreased libido, while moderate-to-severe OSA showed only a borderline association. In the extended model including daytime symptoms and depressive symptoms, higher depressive symptom scores remained independently associated with decreased libido, whereas indices of OSA severity, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue were not associated. Sex-stratified analyses showed that depressive symptoms and relationship status were associated with decreased libido among women, whereas age was the main determinant among men. Formal testing of the interaction between sex and depressive symptoms was not statistically significant.ConclusionsSelf-reported decreased libido is common among patients evaluated for suspected OSA. Decreased libido appears to be more consistently associated with depressive symptoms and psychosocial factors than with objective respiratory disease severity. These findings highlight the importance of integrating psychological and quality-of-life assessment into routine respiratory care pathways for patients evaluated for OSA. In patients evaluated for suspected obstructive sleep apnea, nearly half reported decreased sexual desire. We found that low libido was more strongly associated with depressive symptoms and age than with the severity of sleep apnea. Breathing disturbances during sleep were not independently linked to decreased libido. People living with a partner were more likely to report changes in sexual desire, likely because these changes are more noticeable. These results highlight the importance of considering psychological and social factors, in addition to respiratory measures, when evaluating patients with sleep apnea.

items.title: Durable clinical benefit of nivolumab plus cabozantinib in advanced collecting duct carcinoma: a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge.
items.abstract: Collecting duct carcinoma (CDC) of the kidney is a rare and aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options and a poor prognosis. Diagnostic uncertainty and a lack of prospective evidence frequently complicate clinical management. We describe a case of locally advanced CDC with extensive locoregional involvement and an atypical immunohistochemical profile. Histological diagnosis was challenging and required careful integration of morphologic, immunophenotypic, and clinical-radiological findings. The patient was treated with nivolumab plus cabozantinib, achieving rapid and durable clinical benefit and radiological response. The clinical course was complicated by severe gastrointestinal surgical events, which were successfully managed. Following multidisciplinary discussion, systemic treatment was safely resumed. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of CDC and supports the potential role of combined immunotherapy and tyrosine kinase inhibition in selected patients with advanced disease.

items.title: Circulating alpha-fetoprotein-specific T-cell responses are associated with clinical outcomes after radiofrequency ablation or immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.abstract: Circulating tumor antigen-specific T-cell responses are promising peripheral immune biomarkers associated with treatment efficacy, yet clinical translation is hampered by incomplete epitope maps and non-standardized assays. This study aimed to map the T-cell epitope repertoire of AFP and develop a PBMC-based assay to quantify circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in HCC. CD8+ T-cell epitopes in AFP were screened using in silico prediction, peptide-PBMC coculture, peptide competitive binding assays, and immunization in HLA-transgenic mice, and then applied in clinical cohorts. Totally, 48 CD8+ T-cell epitopes identified here and 20 from our previous study were confirmed immunogenic. These peptides were used to establish an IFN-γ ELISpot assay for quantifying circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in PBMCs. A total of 170 HCC patients with elevated serum AFP were included in two derivation cohorts: 80 patients treated with RFA and 90 receiving anti-PD-1 plus anti-VEGF therapy. In the RFA derivation cohort, the post-treatment/pre-treatment fold of AFP-specific T-cell responses was independently associated with DFS (AUC, 0.838; cutoff, 1.95-fold for DFS >12 vs. ≤12 mo). In the anti-PD-1 plus anti-VEGF derivation cohort, the post-treatment/pre-treatment fold of AFP-specific T-cell responses was independently associated with objective response and 6-month PFS (AUC, 0.850 and 0.863, respectively), with a unified 2.5-fold cutoff for outcome stratification. These findings in the immunotherapy setting were further validated in an independent external cohort of 50 HCC patients with elevated serum AFP receiving combined anti-PD-1 and anti-VEGF therapy. This study establishes an IFN-γ ELISpot assay for quantifying circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in PBMCs and supports their potential translational utility as a novel peripheral immune-monitoring biomarker associated with clinical outcomes in AFP-positive HCC patients.

items.title: Immune control of tumor stemness and therapy resistance.
items.abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSC) are a small group of tumor cells capable of self-renewing, giving rise to new tumors, and resisting treatment, thereby causing recurrence and metastasis and representing a serious clinical problem. However, there are no approved therapies for their elimination, and limited information is available on the effects of current therapies on tumor stemness. A general consensus suggests that the anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment promotes tumor stemness. Since we previously reported that ablation of the p50 NF-κB gene in the hematopoietic compartment (p50fl/flTie2-Cre mice) restores M1/Th1 antitumor immunity, we studied its effects on CSC and therapy resistance in models of fibrosarcoma and melanoma. Using p50fl/flTie2-Cre mice, we demonstrate that p50 NF-κB silencing impairs CSC development, their migratory capacity, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), events known to correlate with tumor aggressiveness. Furthermore, we identify a clear antagonistic effect between Th1 and Th2 T cell polarization, with the former acting as inhibitors and the latter promoting the stemness phenotype. Consistently, while immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 promoted a marked reduction in CSC and tumor development, associated with increased levels of IFNγ, whereas concomitant administration of anti-IFNγ antibodies restored tumor growth and dissemination. Moreover, treatment with anti-IL-4 enhanced the antitumor effects of immunotherapy, reducing tumor cell stemness. Importantly, the antitumor effects of high-dose IFNγ and anti-IL-4 were confirmed in combination with doxorubicin chemotherapy. Overall, our data indicate that shifting the immune response toward a robust M1/Th1 state can significantly improve current immunotherapies and chemotherapies, by limiting CSC properties.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy combined with palliative transarterial chemoembolization followed by targeted therapy and immunotherapy in patients with BCLC stage C hepatocellular carcinoma: Clinical trial protocol.
items.abstract: Interventional therapy combined with systemic treatment has demonstrated promising antitumor activity and an overall manageable safety profile in patients with advanced, unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, prospective evidence supporting the optimal combination strategy remains limited, and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) characteristics underlying differential treatment responses have not been systematically elucidated. The present study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) combined with palliative transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), followed by sequential targeted-immunotherapy, in treatment-naïve patients with BCLC stage C HCC, while also exploring the TIME features associated with therapeutic response. This study is a prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial that will enroll treatment-naïve patients with BCLC C HCC who are unsuitable for surgical resection. Tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples will be collected at baseline prior to treatment initiation. All patients will receive HAIC with a modified FOLFOX regimen combined with palliative TACE. Immediately after the interventional procedure, patients will undergo intra-arterial infusion of bevacizumab (200-300 mg) and intravenous administration of sintilimab (200 mg) every three weeks for a total of six cycles. After two treatment cycles, patients will be stratified according to their treatment response, and five additional tumor tissue and blood samples will be collected from each group. Upon completion of local therapy, patients will continue with maintenance therapy consisting of intravenous bevacizumab (15 mg/kg) and sintilimab (200 mg) every three weeks until disease progression or the development of intolerable toxicity. This study will evaluate the efficacy and safety of HAIC combined with palliative TACE followed by sequential targeted-immunotherapy and explore TIME features associated with treatment response. The findings may provide evidence to inform multimodal treatment strategies and personalized therapy for advanced HCC. ChiCTR2500115704.

items.title: Senolytic drug reduces cancer resistance to PD-L1 blockade.
items.abstract: Resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including anti-PD-L1 therapies, remains a major challenge in cancer treatment, with many patients relapsing despite initial responses. Here, we develop a mathematical model to investigate a mechanism of anti-PD-L1 resistance driven by age-associated senescence of CD8+ T cells, in which senescent T cells (Ts) secrete VEGF, thereby promoting tumor growth through enhanced vascular support. To counteract this effect, we incorporate the senolytic drug navitoclax (ABT-263), which selectively eliminates senescent T cells, and evaluate the efficacy of combined senolytic-anti-PD-L1 therapy in extending tumor remission. Model predictions are validated against independent murine data involving navitoclax and anti-PD-L1 treatment. The model is used to study different strategies of combining the senolytic drug with anti-PD-L1, in order to maximize the remission time of the combined treatment. The optimal starting time of the treatment with the senolytic drug depends on the senescent-to-functional T cells ratio, Ts/T. The paper identifies immune senescence as an important determinant of response to cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Immunosuppressive monocytes promote infection in patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis.
items.abstract: Broad immune cell dysfunction known as immune paralysis is a hallmark of severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH). This process may drive susceptibility to infection and contribute to high short-term mortality in these patients. However, the mechanisms of immune paralysis are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to elucidate the role of myeloid cells in immune dysfunction in severe AH to identify potential biomarkers of infection risk and therapeutic targets. We analyzed the peripheral immune compartment of AH patients, heavy drinkers, and healthy controls and discovered that AH patients at risk for infection had an expanded peripheral monocyte population that was CXCR5+CCR4+ (C-X-C chemokine receptor type 5, C-C chemokine receptor type 4) and had lower activity of pro-inflammatory pathways (eg, Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha, TNF-α, and Interleukin-1 beta, IL-1β) compared with controls. The frequency of circulating CXCR5+CCR4+ monocytes in AH patients negatively correlated with 12-month transplant-free survival. Ex vivo CXCR5+ AH monocytes had reduced phagocytic activity, and they suppressed T-cell proliferation compared with CXCR5- and healthy control monocytes. CXCR5+ AH monocytes expressed PD-L1 (Programmed Death Ligand 1), which is a costimulatory molecule known to inhibit T-cell activation, and TMEM176B (Tolerance-Related and Induced, TORID-1), which is an intracellular cation channel that regulates calcium flux. Inhibition of TORID-1 promoted human monocyte phagocytosis and IL-1β release. CXCR5+CCR4+ monocytes arise in patients with severe AH and have impaired phagocytosis, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and suppress T-cell proliferation. These cells may promote susceptibility to bacterial infection and predict outcomes in severe AH. These may represent novel therapeutic targets to alleviate immune dysfunction in severe AH.

items.title: Monitoring of viral genome occurrence and persistence in municipal wastewater: a one-year study of adenovirus, polyomaviruses, and hepatitis A virus.
items.abstract: Monitoring viruses in wastewater can provide useful information on community-level viral circulation and the persistence of viral genome concentrations after treatment. The present study investigated the occurrence of four viral targets in 72 wastewater samples over a one-year period. The results showed that at least one viral target was detected in 55 of 72 samples (76.4%). HAdV was the most frequently detected virus (48.6%), followed by JCPyV (27.8%), BKPyV (22.2%), and HAV (16.7%). Detection frequencies were generally higher in influent than effluent wastewater for all targets. JCPyV showed the clearest treatment-stage difference, decreasing from 41.7% in influent samples to 13.9% in effluent samples, while HAdV detection decreased from 61.1% in influent to 36.1% in effluent samples. Viral load concentrations were higher in influent than effluent samples for all viral targets. HAdV had nine paired quantifiable influent-effluent observations, with a median treatment-associated reduction of 0.63 log 10 GC/L. Seasonal analysis showed the highest HAdV detection during winter (77.8%), while JCPyV was also most frequently detected in winter (38.9%); HAV detection was more sporadic and occurred mainly during winter and spring. Multi-virus detection occurred in 29.2%, most commonly involving HAdV with JCPyV or BKPyV. Infectivity assessment of 20 HAdV-positive samples showed cytopathic effect in 11 samples; 10 met the predefined combined criterion of CPE plus a ≥ 1-log 10 post-culture increase, with CPE-positive samples showing a median post-culture increase of 1.29 log 10 GC/L. The study supports the assessment of wastewater viral surveillance as a useful complementary tool for environmental virology and public health monitoring.
items.journal: Environmental science and pollution research international

items.title: METTL3 deficiency drives lethal hepatitis via NF-κB-primed NLRP3 inflammasome activation and pyroptosis.
items.abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification plays a crucial role in diverse biological processes. METTL3, the core catalytic subunit of the m6A methyltransferase complex, has been implicated in various liver diseases; however, its intrinsic function in postnatal liver development and the maintenance of hepatic homeostasis remains largely unknown. This study aims to investigate the role of METTL3 in liver development and homeostasis maintenance. Hepatocyte-specific Mettl3 knockout (HKO) mice were generated. Liver injury, inflammation, and fibrosis were assessed at different ages. Mechanistic studies examined NF-κB signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and pyroptosis. Rescue experiments were performed using AAV8-mediated Mettl3 restoration, AAV8-mediated Nlrp3 knockdown, and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition. Mettl3 deficiency triggers spontaneous progressive liver injury from 4 weeks of age, culminating in juvenile lethality by 8 weeks, with extensive hepatic inflammation and fibrosis. Mechanistically, Mettl3 deficiency activates NF-κB signaling, which primes NLRP3 inflammasome expression, leading to pyroptosis driven by caspase - 1 activation and GSDMD cleavage. AAV8-mediated restoration of Mettl3, as well as Nlrp3 knockdown or pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition, substantially ameliorates pyroptosis, hepatic injury, and premature lethality in mice. Moreover, Mettl3 haploinsufficiency sensitizes mice to both ConA-induced acute hepatitis and CCl 4 -induced chronic liver injury, which are effectively prevented by pharmacological NLRP3 blockade. Mettl3 is indispensable for postnatal liver development and homeostasis, with its absence triggering NLRP3-dependent pyroptosis-associated signaling and lethal hepatitis. These findings highlight the METTL3-NF-κB-NLRP3 axis as a promising therapeutic target for inflammatory liver diseases.

items.title: A case of acute hepatitis E associated with Graves' disease.
items.abstract: Hyperthyroidism is a recognized cause of liver injury; however, distinguishing hyperthyroidism-associated liver dysfunction from acute viral hepatitis can be challenging. We report a man in his 50 s who presented with fever, fatigue, marked hyperthyroidism, and severe liver injury. Laboratory tests showed an alanine aminotransferase level of 1534 U/L and total bilirubin level of 12.0 mg/dL. Positive TSH receptor antibody and thyroid-stimulating antibody, together with increased thyroid vascularity on ultrasonography, supported a diagnosis of Graves' disease. Antithyroid treatment improved thyroid hormone levels and liver enzymes, although hyperbilirubinemia persisted. Subsequent testing of the admission sample revealed positive IgA anti-hepatitis E virus (HEV) antibodies, leading to a diagnosis of acute hepatitis E. HEV RNA testing was not performed. Because hyperthyroidism and liver injury were already present at admission, a causal relationship between HEV infection and Graves' disease could not be established. HEV infection and hyperthyroidism may have both contributed to the liver injury. This case highlights the importance of considering HEV infection in acute liver injury accompanied by thyroid dysfunction.

items.title: Hydroxychloroquine as adjunctive therapy in steroid-dependent pediatric Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease with liver dysfunction: A case report.
items.abstract: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is usually self-limiting, but treatment of steroid-dependent disease in children remains uncertain. We report a 7-year-old girl with biopsy-confirmed Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease and severe liver dysfunction. She presented with intermittent fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, followed by rash and worsening liver dysfunction. Cervical lymph node biopsy revealed necrotizing lymphadenitis without evidence of malignancy. Antinuclear and U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies were positive; liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibodies were subsequently detected. Serologic tests for the viruses examined were negative, although hepatitis A testing was not performed. Retrospective assessment using the revised International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group scoring system did not reach the threshold for probable autoimmune hepatitis. Nevertheless, autoimmune hepatitis could not be excluded because liver histology was unavailable and the viral evaluation was incomplete. After relapse during prednisolone tapering, she received methylprednisolone pulse therapy followed by prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine. Remission was achieved, allowing gradual corticosteroid tapering. Prednisolone was discontinued at month 39 and hydroxychloroquine at month 50 after disease onset. No relapse occurred during the subsequent 8-month follow-up. No hydroxychloroquine-related adverse events, including retinopathy, were observed during 44 months of treatment or the subsequent follow-up. This case adds to the limited experience with prolonged hydroxychloroquine use in younger children with steroid-dependent Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease. Hydroxychloroquine may have contributed to corticosteroid tapering, although its independent efficacy cannot be established because it was initiated alongside intensified corticosteroid therapy.

items.title: Longitudinal changes in a blood-based prognostic liver secretome signature and long-term hepatocellular carcinoma risk in cirrhosis.
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk in patients with cirrhosis can be predicted by cross-sectional assessment of biomarkers and/or clinical scores, including the Prognostic Liver Secretome signature (PLSec)-based PAaM score. However, HCC risk may change over time, potentially limiting the accuracy of cross-sectional risk prediction. We aimed to evaluate whether longitudinal changes in HCC risk biomarkers/scores improve upon one-time risk assessment. In this nested case-control study within the multi-center prospective National Cancer Institute HCC Early Detection Strategy (HEDS) cohort of patients with cirrhosis, we evaluated longitudinal changes in PLSec over 1 or 2 years. Paired baseline and follow-up serum samples were available for 31 cases and 93 controls for 1-year changes, and for 25 cases and 75 controls for 2-year changes. Cross-sectional PLSec scores were higher in cases than in controls at baseline, Year 1, and Year 2 (p<0.05). The 2-year change in PLSec score (delta-PLSec-Y2) was higher in cases than in controls (p=0.026; AUROC, 0.65; adjusted odds ratio, 1.47 [95% CI, 1.04-2.15]). In multivariable logistic regression, delta-PLSec-Y2 remained significantly associated with HCC risk (p=0.041) along with baseline PAaM. Longitudinal assessment of PLSec at a 2-year interval may provide additional information to refine cross-sectional HCC risk assessment, warranting further independent validation, evaluation of longer intervals, and exploration of optimal re-testing frequency.

items.title: Personalized 90 Y Dosimetry: A Practical Framework for Intent-based Radioembolization.
items.abstract: Yttrium 90 transarterial radioembolization has evolved from a palliative lobar therapy for advanced liver malignancies into a versatile potentially curative treatment across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) stages, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), and liver metastases. Central to this evolution is the shift from empirical population-based activity prescriptions to personalized dosimetry, tailoring administered activity to each patient's anatomy, tumor biology, treatment intent, and microsphere distribution to optimize tumor absorbed dose while constraining normal tissue exposure. Prospective studies have demonstrated that personalized dosimetry significantly improves tumor response and overall survival compared with conventional dosing. Despite this evidence, clinical adoption remains inconsistent. In this review, the authors aim to address that gap by providing a practical intent-based framework for implementation. They present dosimetric principles, activity prescription methods, and dose-response evidence across HCC, iCCA, and liver metastases, with practical recommendations organized by treatment intent. Treatment intent, whether curative or palliative, is the primary determinant of dosimetric strategy, guiding selection of the dosimetry model, target dose, and normal liver dose constraints. The authors review pretreatment planning work flows and posttreatment verification and present a practical decision algorithm integrating clinical intent, imaging, and dosimetry modeling. © RSNA, 2026 See the invited commentary by Malone and Toskich in this issue.
items.journal: Radiographics : a review publication of the Radiological Society of North America, Inc

items.title: Organoids as Functional Models of Hepatic Tropism in Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis: From a Selective Hepatic Niche to Liver-specific Vulnerabilities.
items.abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) is favored by portal anatomy but determined by a sequence of organ-selective bottlenecks: sinusoidal arrest, early survival, immune escape, metabolic accommodation, and growth-pattern-specific expansion. This Review integrates direct human CRLM evidence, mechanistic models, and organoid studies to define what is established, what remains inferential, and what next-generation models must test. Paired primary-tumor and liver-metastasis organoids preserve inter- and intrapatient heterogeneity and can reproduce selected chemotherapy responses, but epithelial-only cultures cannot model hepatic receptivity. Liver-containing systems should therefore be built as question-specific modules that add hepatocytes, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, hepatic stellate cells, Kupffer or recruited myeloid cells, extracellular matrix, and flow only when required by the hypothesis. We propose an evidence-linked experimental framework combining longitudinal single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin profiling, metabolomics, isotope tracing, spatial readouts, and perturbation-rescue experiments. Particular emphasis is placed on extracellular-vesicle-mediated premetastatic niche formation, clinically observed microenvironmental evolution, and context-dependent vulnerabilities such as vessel co-option and liver-restricted immune-metabolic dependencies. We also define minimum reporting and validation standards required before organoid results can influence clinical decisions. The central conclusion is that organoids become models of hepatic tropism only when liver context is treated as a controlled causal variable rather than as the site from which tumor epithelium was sampled.
